episodes.title: Brains vs Hands: How to Run AI Agents Safely in Production — Viren Baraiya
episodes.description:
Let the model decide what should happen next. Never let it improvise how a production cluster gets restarted.

Viren Baraiya, co-founder and CTO of Orkes and the original creator of Netflix Conductor, explains how to run agents in production. Real agents aren't just chatbots: they run on schedules, react to events, coordinate other agents and can run for months, so the harness around them starts to look like an application, much like a set of microservices. His key idea is a clean split between the brain and the hands. The LLM plans what should happen next; a deterministic, durable harness does the actual work, with approval gates, idempotent steps and recorded side effects. He frames agent harnesses as late-bound sagas, workflows the agent assembles at runtime, and demos an SRE agent whose plan is compiled into a Conductor workflow, executed, checked and re-planned over two loops.

In this talk:
• Background, scheduled, event-driven and long-running agents
• Why the harness is the application, mixing deterministic and non-deterministic parts
• The brain and the hands: the LLM plans, the harness executes
• Demo: an SRE agent's plan compiled into a durable workflow

episodes.title: We Mapped 115 Microservices for Our Coding Agents — Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Postman
episodes.description:
Coding agents are great inside one repo. Postman has 115 microservices and thousands of endpoints.

Kamalakannan Nandagopal, staff engineer at Postman, shares how Postman made coding agents work across a real distributed system. Docs go stale, skills and MCPs are only as good as their context, and agent memory stays stuck with one person. Borrowing from Postman's go-to-market team, they realized APIs are the context layer, and built an API context graph that maps every service, endpoint, implementation and call, all the way down to databases, with every data point grounded in code or production telemetry. He shares evals built from real PRs and design decisions: big wins on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment, an honest failure when the graph went stale, the finding that 75% of PRs touched APIs, and a 21-page architecture review the agent produced on its own.

In this talk:
• Why coding agents struggle with distributed systems and microservices
• Building an API context graph grounded in code and telemetry
• Eval results on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment
• Why keeping the graph fresh matters as much as building it

episodes.title: Turning Agent Memory Into Skills That Work — Will Lyon, Neo4j
episodes.description:
Agents finish a task, then forget what they learned. Retrieval alone won't fix that.

Will Lyon, senior product manager at Neo4j, explains why agent memory built on embeddings and retrieval isn't enough: recall isn't actionable knowledge. Agents need knowledge that is connected, typed and traceable. He shows Neo4j's model of agent memory as a context graph with short-term, long-term and reasoning memory, covering entity extraction and resolution, shared ontologies, and decision traces that let many agents learn from each other. Then he turns memory into action: distilling grounded, governed skills from the graph, based on Neo4j research that treats skills as typed execution graphs, with checks for grounding, coverage and coherence, and alerts when a skill goes stale. He demos the Neo4j Agent Memory Service distilling a patient-intake skill from a healthcare conversation.

In this talk:
• Why retrieval isn't actionable knowledge
• Short-term, long-term and reasoning memory in one context graph
• Distilling grounded, governed skills from memory
• Demo: the Neo4j Agent Memory Service building a skill from a conversation

episodes.title: Why We Deleted Our MCP Server and Rebuilt It — Abhi Arya, Reducto
episodes.description:
Reducto gave its whole team an MCP server with a tool for every endpoint. It broke the same day.

Abhi Arya, who works on product at Reducto, argues that building agent-first software comes down to one question: who pays when the agent is wrong? He describes three approaches, auto mode, user-first, and agent experience in service of the user, and how Reducto learned the difference. A first MCP server with one tool per API endpoint demoed well but fell apart when the whole team used it: the agent built entire workflows confidently, and nobody could explain them. He deleted it in one commit and rebuilt with fewer tools that carry the structure of real work, plus a snapshot tool for live state. Then he made uncertainty visible, with confidence scores and an agent that asks instead of guessing, and added instrumentation that made the system improve on its own, until the sales team adopted it without being asked.

In this talk:
• Auto mode vs user-first vs agent experience in service of the user
• Why one tool per API endpoint fails, and what to build instead
• Making uncertainty visible: confidence scores and asking instead of guessing
• Instrumentation that turns usage into a self-improving loop

episodes.title: Let Anyone at Your Company Ship Internal Apps with AI — Garrett Galow, WorkOS
episodes.description:
Building an app with AI got cheap. Getting it in front of your coworkers didn't.

Garrett Galow from the WorkOS product team shows how WorkOS lets anyone at the company build and ship internal apps. It started when an account executive built a helpful sales chatbot before her leave, and the CEO couldn't even open it. Building got cheap with AI, but deploying, securing and sharing apps still needed engineers. So WorkOS built two things: WOW, a CLI pushed to every laptop that sets up the repo, tools and template in one command, and Atlas, the platform underneath, which keeps infrastructure invisible, makes every app secure by default behind company SSO, and makes every app discoverable. He demos it live and shares results: 278 apps, more than 3 million requests a week, and 37% of regularly used apps built with no engineer in a single commit.

In this talk:
• Why shipping, not building, is now the bottleneck for internal tools
• Claude days: pairing non-engineers at the keyboard with engineers as coaches
• A one-command CLI and a platform that's invisible, secure and discoverable
• Results: hundreds of apps, millions of requests, many built without engineers

episodes.title: Giving AI Agents Memory That Learns — Jake Broekhuizen, LangChain
episodes.description:
Most teams are great at watching what their agents did. Far fewer turn that into lessons for the next run.

Jake Broekhuizen from LangChain's Labs team explains how to give agents memory that actually changes their behavior. Using a real financial services agent whose tone kept slipping from advisory to pushy, he shows why traces and logs are only evidence: they become memory only when a lesson turns into durable context the agent reads next time. He breaks memory into semantic, episodic and procedural types, separates working memory from long-term memory, and walks through the read-write cycle: read context, run, filter the evidence for signal, and write it back. He shows how LangSmith and Context Hub capture, analyze and update that context, and shares three hard-won lessons about what to keep, caching, and when a human should review changes.

In this talk:
• Why observability alone doesn't make an agent improve
• Semantic, episodic and procedural memory, and which one moves behavior most
• The read-write cycle: run, filter evidence for signal, update context
• Lessons: most traces stay history, watch caching, review procedural changes

episodes.title: Why Bigger Context Windows Won't Save Your Agent — Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, AWS
episodes.description:
A bigger context window won't save your agent. Past a point, it forgets the middle.

Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, developer advocate at AWS, explains why agents break when tools return huge amounts of data, and why bigger context windows aren't the fix: models remember the start and end of a long context but lose the middle. Using the open-source, model-agnostic Strands Agents framework, she walks through four strategies (externalize, select, compress, isolate) with code. She covers sliding-window and summarizing conversation managers, short-term, long-term and graph memory, memory pointers that keep big tool outputs out of context, sharing pointers across a swarm of agents, capping tool calls to stop endless loops, and async handles for slow MCP tools. She ends with the anti-patterns to avoid.

In this talk:
• Why bigger context windows don't fix agents, and how models lose the middle
• Four strategies: externalize, select, compress and isolate
• Memory pointers, conversation managers and multi-agent state in Strands
• Stopping endless tool loops and handling slow MCP tools

episodes.title: AI Hackers Are Faster Than Your Pen Test — Eli Cohen, Snyk
episodes.description:
Attackers use AI too, and the fastest AI attack he cites took four minutes. A pen test once or twice a year can't keep up.

Eli Cohen of Snyk, co-founder of the runtime security company Helios, explains why security has to go on the offense in an agent-first world. Developers now ship far more code, much of it insecure, while attackers use frontier models to chain small vulnerabilities into critical ones in minutes. He walks through why traditional tools fall short: static scanning misses runtime issues, dynamic testing misses business logic, and human pen tests are expensive and happen only a few times a year. Then he describes continuous offensive security: AI pen testing on every code change, agent red teaming, and a team of agents (orchestrator, recon, vulnerability hunters, an exploit-validating judge, remediation and reporting), fed with context from other scanners. He ends with four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor.

In this talk:
• Why AI-generated code and AI-powered attackers break the old security model
• SAST vs DAST vs pen testing, and what each one misses
• How a team of agents runs pen tests and proves exploits on every PR
• Four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor

episodes.title: Why Your AI Agents Can't Talk to Each Other (Yet) — Vlad Luzin, BAND
episodes.description:
If you run Claude and Codex side by side, you're the router passing messages between them. It doesn't have to be that way.

Vlad Luzin, co-founder and CTO of BAND, argues the future belongs to AI agents talking to other AI agents, inside companies, between companies, and between businesses and consumers. Most of us already run multi-agent systems by hand, copying output between a planning session and a reviewing session, and loop engineering just hands that job to a script. He explains why: a single agent suffers from confirmation bias and attention dilution, no matter how big its context. Then he explains why messaging apps and protocols like MCP and A2A don't solve it, and why connecting agents is a distributed systems problem: ordered real-time transport, persistence, runtime binding, identity and observability. He finishes by launching BAND's interaction layer, with demos of agents onboarding in seconds and Claude Code and Codex working together across users.

In this talk:
• Adversarial agents, loop engineering, and the single-agent bottleneck
• Why Slack, Telegram, MCP and A2A fall short for agent-to-agent work
• What connecting agents really takes: transport, persistence, runtime binding
• Demo: Claude Code, Codex and LangGraph agents collaborating across users

episodes.title: Why AI Agents Should Have Their Own Sandbox — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
episodes.description:
Your agent shouldn't run on your laptop. Give it its own computer in the cloud, with one API call.

Philipp Schmid from Google DeepMind walks through the Gemini Interactions API, Google's new API for both models and agents. It handles server-side state, long-running background jobs, and built-in plus custom tools across text, audio and images, and it replaces user/model turns with a timeline of steps. Then he shows the Antigravity agent in the Gemini API, which runs the same harness as Antigravity in its own managed cloud sandbox. Agents can run code, install tools, share environments with other agents and pick up skills and AGENTS.md files automatically. He covers the Agents API for packaging reusable agents, the new Gemini API CLI, and demos an AI talk radio show generated from one prompt.

In this talk:
• The Interactions API: one interface for models and agents
• Why steps replace user/model turns for agentic apps
• Managed sandboxes: persistent, shareable environments with skills built in
• Demo: an AI talk radio agent built from an AGENTS.md file and skills
